title: Moving exams online betrays working-class pupils
author: David James
summary: David James, a deputy head teacher, argues against the digitisation of GCSEs and A-levels, responding to AQA CEO Colin Hughes' claim that there are 'almost no downsides' to moving exams from pen-and-paper to screens. James identifies the core objection as moral rather than logistical: pupils without home device access would be severely disadvantaged by a sudden switch to keyboard-based assessment, while pupils at well-resourced schools and with affluent parents would gain further advantage. Paper exams are defended on grounds of equity—every candidate demonstrates the same skills under the same conditions—while screen exams introduce variance in hardware quality, keyboard proficiency, and access. The practical consequences compound the equity problem: computers crash, screens can be seen by adjacent candidates, and managing 300 students on laptops simultaneously is logistically untenable. James warns that making online exams work would likely require changing the exam format itself—AQA has already proposed 'short-answer text boxes' that would disadvantage students aiming for the highest grades. The closing argument: not every innovation is progress, and before abandoning a system whose strengths are simplicity, reliability, and fairness, there must be demonstrable evidence that the replacement is better—currently absent.
points: The primary objection to online GCSEs is moral: pupils without home device access who have done all classwork by hand would be suddenly disadvantaged against peers at device-equipped schools whose parents can afford touch-typing lessons.

Paper exams are defended as the fairest assessment format because they require every candidate to demonstrate the same skills under identical conditions—a standard that screen-based exams cannot replicate given differences in hardware, connectivity, and typing proficiency.

Practical logistics make the transition untenable: computer malfunction is already a problem for students with special needs using laptops, and managing 300 simultaneous laptop exams—with screens visible to neighbors and devices capable of crashing—represents an enormous operational and security risk.
quotes: The greatest objection is not logistical but moral. The change would not be fair for the many pupils who do not have access to devices at home.

To ask them suddenly to switch to using a keyboard, even though most of their classwork has been handwritten, would seriously damage their prospects of attaining the grades they need. In contrast, pupils who attend schools able to provide devices from the moment a child joins, and whose parents can afford touch-typing lessons, will once again be advantaged by online assessments.
a paper examination asks every candidate to demonstrate the same skills under the same conditions.

Computers can malfunction, and we already see this with pupils with special educational needs who use laptops. Now imagine nearly 300 pupils completing an examination on laptops, each able to see other screens, each device capable of crashing and work being lost.

Not every innovation represents progress. Before we abandon an examination system whose strengths are simplicity, reliability and fairness, we should be certain that any replacement is demonstrably better.
Technology undoubtedly has an important place in education, but fairness must always come first.
